notes: Reasoning Ability part of BATCH_001: 200 original questions (60 Basic, 80 Intermediate, 60 Advanced) built by tools/batch_001/reasoning.py. Puzzles and seating are brute-forced for a unique arrangement; syllogisms are checked over every Venn-region model; inequalities over all integer assignments; data sufficiency by enumerating models for each statement subset; blood relations, directions, coding, series, ranking and input-output are recomputed in code. Verbal-reasoning items (assumptions, conclusions, cause-effect, critical reasoning) are hand-written and independently re-checked. All questions await human review.

stimuli.title: Six friends in a row facing north
stimuli.content:
Six friends Anil, Bina, Chetan, Divya, Eshan and Farah sit in a straight row, all facing north.

- Divya sits at one of the extreme ends of the row.
- Exactly two persons sit between Divya and Chetan.
- Bina sits immediately to the right of Chetan.
- Anil sits third to the left of Farah.
- Farah does not sit at an extreme end of the row.
stimuli.solution:
If Divya sits at the left end (1), Chetan is at 4 and Bina at 5; the only free pair three apart is (3, 6), so Farah would sit at the right end, which is not allowed. Hence Divya sits at the right end (6), Chetan at 3 and Bina at 4. Of the free seats 1, 2 and 5, only (2, 5) are three apart, so Anil is at 2 and Farah at 5, leaving seat 1 for Eshan.

| Seat (from left) | Person |
|---|---|
| 1 | Eshan |
| 2 | Anil |
| 3 | Chetan |
| 4 | Bina |
| 5 | Farah |
| 6 | Divya |

stimuli.title: Eight persons in a row facing north or south
stimuli.content:
Eight persons Gaurav, Hema, Ishaan, Jaya, Kunal, Lata, Mohit and Nidhi sit in a straight row. Some of them face north and the others face south. (For a person facing north, the right is towards the east; for a person facing south, the right is towards the west.)

- Kunal sits at one of the extreme ends of the row and faces south.
- Exactly three persons sit between Kunal and Jaya.
- Ishaan sits immediately to the left of Jaya.
- Ishaan and Jaya face opposite directions.
- Mohit is an immediate neighbour of Kunal and faces the same direction as Kunal.
- Hema sits immediately to the right of Nidhi.
- Lata sits second to the right of Ishaan.
- Only one person sits between Mohit and Hema.
- Hema faces north, and Nidhi faces the same direction as Hema.
- Gaurav and Lata face opposite directions.
- The two persons sitting at the extreme ends of the row face opposite directions.
stimuli.solution:
Kunal is at an end facing south, with Mohit beside him also facing south. Case 1, Kunal at the east end (seat 8): Mohit = 7, Jaya = 4 and Hema = 5. Nidhi faces north, so Hema (on her right) would put Nidhi at seat 4, which is Jaya's: rejected. Case 2, Kunal at the west end (seat 1): Mohit = 2, Jaya = 5, Hema = 4 and Nidhi = 3 (both facing north). Ishaan is immediately to Jaya's left: if Jaya faced north her left would be seat 4 (Hema), so Jaya faces south and Ishaan is at seat 6 facing north. Lata is second to Ishaan's right: seat 8. Gaurav takes seat 7. The ends face opposite ways, so Lata faces north and Gaurav (opposite to Lata) faces south.

| Seat (west to east) | Person | Faces |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Kunal | south |
| 2 | Mohit | south |
| 3 | Nidhi | north |
| 4 | Hema | north |
| 5 | Jaya | south |
| 6 | Ishaan | north |
| 7 | Gaurav | south |
| 8 | Lata | north |

stimuli.title: Ten persons in two facing rows
stimuli.content:
Ten persons Oviya, Pranav, Rekha, Sahil, Tanvi, Uday, Vimal, Wasim, Yamini and Zoya sit in two parallel rows of five seats each, with equal distance between neighbours. Row 1 is to the north and the persons in it face south; Row 2 is to the south and the persons in it face north. So every person faces exactly one person of the other row. Who sits in which row is not given.

- Sahil sits in the middle of the row that faces north.
- The person who faces Sahil sits second to the right of Pranav.
- Pranav sits at one of the extreme ends of a row.
- Oviya faces the person who sits immediately to the right of Tanvi.
- Uday and Vimal sit in the same row with exactly one person between them.
- Zoya faces Vimal.
- Rekha faces Wasim.
- Yamini sits immediately to the right of Zoya.
- Wasim is not an immediate neighbour of Sahil.
- Oviya sits in the same row as Sahil, and Wasim sits in the same row as Yamini.
stimuli.solution:
Sahil is at seat 3 of Row 2, so the person facing him is at seat 3 of Row 1; that person is second to Pranav's right, so Pranav is in Row 1 at the east end (a south-facing person's right is west). Zoya faces Vimal, Yamini sits beside Zoya, Wasim shares Yamini's row and Rekha faces Wasim, so {Zoya, Yamini, Wasim} sit in one row and {Vimal, Uday, Rekha} in the other. If Zoya, Yamini and Wasim were in Row 1, Uday and Vimal would take Row 2 seats 2 and 4, Oviya would be forced to seat 1 (Tanvi at Row 1 seat 2), Zoya would have to face Vimal from seat 4 (seat 2 is Tanvi's), putting Yamini at seat 3 and Wasim at seat 1, and Rekha, facing Wasim, would need Oviya's seat: rejected. So Row 2 holds Sahil, Oviya, Zoya, Yamini and Wasim, and Row 1 holds Pranav, Tanvi, Uday, Vimal and Rekha. Testing Zoya–Yamini at seats 1–2 or 4–5 of Row 2 against the remaining conditions leaves only the arrangement below.

| Seat (west to east) | Row 1 (faces south) | Row 2 (faces north) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Rekha | Wasim |
| 2 | Uday | Oviya |
| 3 | Tanvi | Sahil |
| 4 | Vimal | Zoya |
| 5 | Pranav | Yamini |

stimuli.title: Six friends around a circular table
stimuli.content:
Six friends Kavya, Lalit, Meera, Naveen, Omkar and Priya sit around a circular table, equally spaced, all facing the centre.

- Meera sits immediately to the right of Kavya.
- Lalit sits opposite Kavya.
- Naveen sits second to the right of Lalit.
- Omkar is not an immediate neighbour of Naveen.
stimuli.solution:
Place Kavya first. Meera is immediately to her right and Lalit opposite her. Naveen is second to Lalit's right, which is the seat immediately to Kavya's left. Two seats remain: the one between Meera and Lalit, and the one between Lalit and Naveen. Omkar cannot sit next to Naveen, so Omkar sits between Meera and Lalit and Priya between Lalit and Naveen.

| Order to the right of Kavya | Person |
|---|---|
| 0 | Kavya |
| 1 | Meera |
| 2 | Omkar |
| 3 | Lalit |
| 4 | Priya |
| 5 | Naveen |

stimuli.title: Eight persons around a circle, facing in or out
stimuli.content:
Eight persons Aarav, Bhavna, Chirag, Deepa, Farhan, Gita, Harsh and Isha sit around a circular table, equally spaced. Some of them face the centre and the others face outside. (For a person facing the centre, the right is anticlockwise; for a person facing outside, the right is clockwise.)

- Farhan sits opposite Aarav.
- Aarav faces the centre, and Gita sits immediately to his right.
- Gita and Aarav face opposite directions.
- Harsh sits third to the right of Isha.
- Harsh and Farhan face the same direction.
- Deepa is an immediate neighbour of Aarav.
- Chirag sits second to the right of Farhan.
- Bhavna is an immediate neighbour of both Farhan and Harsh.
- Exactly three persons face outside.
- Isha faces the same direction as Aarav.
stimuli.solution:
Fix Aarav (facing the centre). Farhan is opposite him, Gita is the next seat anticlockwise (facing outside) and Deepa takes the other seat beside Aarav. Bhavna sits between Farhan and Harsh: either (a) Bhavna and Harsh on Gita's side of Farhan, or (b) on Deepa's side. In (a) Harsh is next to Gita, Chirag must be two seats from Farhan on Deepa's side (so Farhan faces the centre), Isha takes the last seat, and Harsh being third to Isha's right forces Isha to face outside, contradicting 'Isha faces the same way as Aarav'. In (b) Chirag is two seats from Farhan on Gita's side, so Farhan faces outside, and so does Harsh. Isha takes the seat between Chirag and Farhan; counting three to her right reaches Harsh only if she faces the centre. Gita, Farhan and Harsh are the three facing outside, so everyone else faces the centre.

| Anticlockwise from Aarav | Person | Faces |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Aarav | centre |
| 1 | Gita | outside |
| 2 | Chirag | centre |
| 3 | Isha | centre |
| 4 | Farhan | outside |
| 5 | Bhavna | centre |
| 6 | Harsh | outside |
| 7 | Deepa | centre |

stimuli.title: Eight persons at a square table, with home cities
stimuli.content:
Eight persons Jatin, Komal, Lokesh, Manju, Neel, Pallavi, Rohan and Sneha sit around a square table. Four of them sit at the four corners and face the centre; the other four sit at the middle of the four sides and face outside (away from the centre). Each of them is from a different city among Agra, Bhopal, Cochin, Dehradun, Indore, Jaipur, Kanpur and Mysuru.

- The person from Bhopal sits opposite Jatin.
- Lokesh sits second to the right of the person from Bhopal.
- Sneha is from Agra.
- Rohan faces the centre and sits immediately to the left of the person from Agra.
- Komal is from Jaipur and is an immediate neighbour of both Rohan and Manju.
- Jatin sits second to the left of the person from Mysuru.
- Neel is from Kanpur and sits opposite Sneha.
- The person from Cochin sits immediately to the right of the person from Dehradun.
- The persons from Dehradun and Indore both face the centre.
stimuli.solution:
Rohan faces the centre (a corner) and sits immediately to the left of Sneha (Agra). If Sneha were at a corner, her immediate left would be a side seat, so Sneha sits at a side, facing outside, with Rohan on the next corner to her left. Komal (Jaipur) sits on Rohan's other side, with Manju at the following corner. Neel (Kanpur) sits opposite Sneha, i.e. on the side after Manju. Jatin is second to the left of the Mysuru person and the Bhopal person sits opposite Jatin; together with Lokesh being second to the right of the Bhopal person, this places Jatin at the corner on Sneha's other side, Manju (Bhopal) opposite him, Lokesh at the last corner and Rohan from Mysuru. Pallavi takes the last side seat. Dehradun faces the centre and Cochin is immediately to its right, so Lokesh is from Dehradun and Pallavi from Cochin; Indore (a corner) goes to Jatin.

| Anticlockwise from Jatin | Person | City | Seat type |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | Jatin | Indore | corner (faces centre) |
| 1 | Sneha | Agra | side (faces outside) |
| 2 | Rohan | Mysuru | corner (faces centre) |
| 3 | Komal | Jaipur | side (faces outside) |
| 4 | Manju | Bhopal | corner (faces centre) |
| 5 | Neel | Kanpur | side (faces outside) |
| 6 | Lokesh | Dehradun | corner (faces centre) |
| 7 | Pallavi | Cochin | side (faces outside) |

stimuli.title: Six persons on six floors
stimuli.content:
Six persons Tara, Usha, Varun, Wamiq, Yogita and Zubin live on the six floors of a building, one on each floor. The lowermost floor is numbered 1 and the topmost floor is numbered 6.

- Tara lives on an odd-numbered floor.
- Only one person lives between Tara and Usha.
- Wamiq lives immediately above Usha.
- Zubin lives immediately above Tara, but below Usha.
- Varun lives on a floor below Yogita.
- Yogita does not live on the topmost floor.
stimuli.solution:
Tara is on 1, 3 or 5 with Zubin immediately above her and Usha above Zubin. Tara = 1 gives Usha = 3, Wamiq = 4, Zubin = 2, leaving floors 5 and 6 for Varun and Yogita, so Yogita would be on the top floor: rejected. Tara = 5 puts Zubin on 6, above every possible Usha: rejected. So Tara = 3, Zubin = 4, Usha = 5 (floor 1 would be below Zubin), Wamiq = 6, and Varun = 1, Yogita = 2.

| Floor | Person |
|---|---|
| 6 | Wamiq |
| 5 | Usha |
| 4 | Zubin |
| 3 | Tara |
| 2 | Yogita |
| 1 | Varun |

stimuli.title: Eight persons in a four-storey building with two flats per floor
stimuli.content:
Eight persons Arjun, Bindu, Cyrus, Daksh, Ekta, Firoz, Gauri and Hiten live in a four-storey building. The lowermost floor is 1 and the topmost is 4. Each floor has two flats, West and East; the West flat of a floor is directly above the West flat of the floor below it, and likewise for the East flats. Each person lives in a different flat.

- Daksh lives in a West flat on an odd-numbered floor, but not on the lowermost floor.
- Bindu lives in the flat immediately above Hiten's flat.
- Hiten and Daksh live on the same floor.
- Cyrus lives in an East flat, immediately below Ekta's flat.
- Arjun and Ekta live on the same floor.
- Firoz lives on a floor below Gauri's floor.
stimuli.solution:
Daksh is on floor 3, West flat. Hiten shares his floor, so Hiten is in 3-East and Bindu, directly above Hiten, is in 4-East. Ekta has Cyrus directly below her in an East flat; 4-East and 3-East are taken, so Ekta is in 2-East and Cyrus in 1-East. Arjun shares Ekta's floor: 2-West. Firoz and Gauri take 1-West and 4-West, and Firoz is lower, so Firoz = 1-West and Gauri = 4-West.

| Floor | West flat | East flat |
|---|---|---|
| 4 | Gauri | Bindu |
| 3 | Daksh | Hiten |
| 2 | Arjun | Ekta |
| 1 | Firoz | Cyrus |

stimuli.title: Seven persons on seven floors with favourite sports
stimuli.content:
Seven persons Jai, Kiran, Leela, Manav, Nisha, Ojas and Puja live on the seven floors of a building, one on each floor (floor 1 is the lowermost, floor 7 the topmost). Each likes a different sport among Badminton, Chess, Cricket, Hockey, Kabaddi, Tennis and Volleyball.

- Jai lives on an odd-numbered floor above floor 3 and likes Kabaddi.
- Only two persons live between Jai and the person who likes Hockey.
- Ojas likes Hockey, and the person who likes Tennis lives immediately above Ojas.
- Manav likes Volleyball and lives below Leela.
- Puja lives immediately below Jai and likes Cricket.
- The person who likes Chess lives on the lowermost floor.
- Leela does not like Tennis.
- Kiran lives above Nisha, and Leela lives above Jai.
stimuli.solution:
Jai is on 5 or 7; Leela lives above him, so Jai = 5 and Puja (Cricket) = 4. Hockey is three floors from Jai: floor 2 (8 does not exist), so Ojas = 2 and Tennis = 3. Chess is on floor 1. Floors 1, 3, 6 and 7 remain for Kiran, Leela, Manav and Nisha. Manav likes Volleyball, so he is not on 1 (Chess) or 3 (Tennis); with Leela above him, Manav = 6 and Leela = 7. Kiran is above Nisha: Nisha = 1 (Chess), Kiran = 3 (Tennis). Leela gets the remaining sport, Badminton.

| Floor | Person | Sport |
|---|---|---|
| 7 | Leela | Badminton |
| 6 | Manav | Volleyball |
| 5 | Jai | Kabaddi |
| 4 | Puja | Cricket |
| 3 | Kiran | Tennis |
| 2 | Ojas | Hockey |
| 1 | Nisha | Chess |

stimuli.title: Eight persons in a nine-storey building with one vacant floor
stimuli.content:
A building has nine floors, numbered 1 (lowermost) to 9 (topmost). Eight persons Raghav, Simran, Tushar, Ujjwala, Vedant, Waheeda, Yuvraj and Zeenat live in it, one on each floor, so exactly one floor is vacant. Each person likes a different fruit among Apple, Banana, Cherry, Guava, Kiwi, Mango, Orange and Papaya.

- The vacant floor is an even-numbered floor above floor 4.
- Tushar lives immediately below the vacant floor and likes Banana.
- Exactly two floors lie between Tushar's floor and the floor of the person who likes Mango.
- Vedant likes Mango and lives below Tushar.
- The person who likes Papaya lives immediately above Zeenat, who lives on an odd-numbered floor.
- Simran lives below Vedant.
- Exactly one floor lies between Ujjwala's floor and Waheeda's floor.
- Ujjwala lives above the vacant floor, and Yuvraj lives immediately above Ujjwala.
- Yuvraj likes Orange, and the person who likes Guava lives immediately below him.
- The person who likes Cherry lives above the person who likes Guava.
- The person who likes Kiwi lives below the person who likes Apple.
- Raghav lives above Simran, and the number of floors between Simran and Raghav is the same as the number of floors between Raghav and Ujjwala.
stimuli.solution:
The vacant floor is 6 or 8. If it were 8, Tushar = 7 and Ujjwala (above the vacant floor) = 9 would leave no floor for Yuvraj above her: so the vacant floor is 6 and Tushar (Banana) = 5. Mango is three floors from Tushar and below him: Vedant (Mango) = 2, so Simran = 1. Ujjwala is on 7 or 8 with Yuvraj above; Ujjwala = 8 would put Waheeda on 6 (vacant) or 10, so Ujjwala = 7, Yuvraj (Orange) = 8 and Waheeda = 9. Raghav is midway between Simran (1) and Ujjwala (7): floor 4. Zeenat takes the odd floor 3, with Papaya (Raghav) above her. Guava is immediately below Orange: Ujjwala. Cherry is above Guava: Waheeda. Apple and Kiwi remain for Zeenat and Simran; Kiwi is lower, so Simran likes Kiwi and Zeenat Apple.

| Floor | Person | Fruit |
|---|---|---|
| 9 | Waheeda | Cherry |
| 8 | Yuvraj | Orange |
| 7 | Ujjwala | Guava |
| 6 | (vacant) | - |
| 5 | Tushar | Banana |
| 4 | Raghav | Papaya |
| 3 | Zeenat | Apple |
| 2 | Vedant | Mango |
| 1 | Simran | Kiwi |

stimuli.title: Six boxes in a stack
stimuli.content:
Six boxes P, Q, R, S, T and U are kept one above another in a single stack. Position 1 is the bottom and position 6 the top.

- Box R is kept immediately above box U.
- Only one box is kept between box R and box T, and box T is above box R.
- Box P is kept immediately above box S.
- Box P is kept below box U.
- Box Q is not kept adjacent to box U.
stimuli.solution:
U, R and T follow the pattern U, R, (one box), T, so U is at 1, 2 or 3. P sits on S and below U, so S and P need two positions under U: U = 3, R = 4, T = 6, S = 1, P = 2. Q takes position 5.

| Position | Box |
|---|---|
| 6 | T |
| 5 | Q |
| 4 | R |
| 3 | U |
| 2 | P |
| 1 | S |

stimuli.title: Seven coloured boxes in a stack
stimuli.content:
Seven boxes K, L, M, N, O, P and Q are kept one above another in a single stack (position 1 is the bottom, 7 the top). Each box is of a different colour among Black, Blue, Green, Pink, Red, White and Yellow.

- The green box is kept exactly in the middle of the stack, and box P is green.
- Box O is kept above box P, with exactly two boxes between them.
- Box L is pink and is kept immediately below box O.
- The red box is kept immediately above box N.
- Box K is kept immediately below the green box and is not red.
- Only one box is kept between box K and the white box.
- The yellow box is kept immediately above the green box.
- Box Q is kept below box M.
- The blue box is kept above the pink box.
stimuli.solution:
P (green) is at 4, so O = 7, L (pink) = 6, K = 3 and yellow = 5. Blue is above pink, so O is blue. White is two away from K: position 1 or 5, and 5 is yellow, so white = 1. Positions 1, 2 and 5 remain for M, N and Q. Red is immediately above N: N = 1 gives red = 2 (N = 2 would make K red, N = 5 would make L red). So N is white and red is at 2. Q is below M, so Q = 2 (red) and M = 5 (yellow); K is black.

| Position | Box | Colour |
|---|---|---|
| 7 | O | Blue |
| 6 | L | Pink |
| 5 | M | Yellow |
| 4 | P | Green |
| 3 | K | Black |
| 2 | Q | Red |
| 1 | N | White |

stimuli.title: Nine coloured boxes in a stack
stimuli.content:
Nine boxes A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H and I are kept one above another in a single stack (position 1 is the bottom, 9 the top). Each box is of a different colour among Blue, Brown, Green, Grey, Indigo, Orange, Red, Violet and Yellow.

- Box A is kept immediately below the yellow box.
- Three boxes are kept between box A and box G.
- Box G is blue, and box E is kept immediately above it.
- The orange box is kept above box I.
- The number of boxes above box I is the same as the number of boxes below it.
- Box D is green and is kept immediately above box I.
- Only one box is kept between box D and box G.
- The violet box is kept immediately below the blue box.
- Box C is indigo and is kept above box F.
- Only one box is kept between box C and box A.
- Box H is red, and the brown box is kept immediately above it.
- The grey box is kept below the red box.
stimuli.solution:
I has four boxes above and four below: I = 5, so D (green) = 6. G is two from D: 4 or 8. If G = 4, A (four away) = 8 and E (above G) = 5 = I: rejected. So G (blue) = 8, E = 9, A = 4 and yellow = 5 (I). Violet = 7. C is two from A: 2 (6 is D), so C (indigo) = 2 and F (below C) = 1. B and H take 3 and 7; the brown box sits on red H, and 8 is blue, so H = 3 (red), A is brown and B = 7 (violet). Grey is below red: F. The last colour, orange, goes to E, which is above I as required.

| Position | Box | Colour |
|---|---|---|
| 9 | E | Orange |
| 8 | G | Blue |
| 7 | B | Violet |
| 6 | D | Green |
| 5 | I | Yellow |
| 4 | A | Brown |
| 3 | H | Red |
| 2 | C | Indigo |
| 1 | F | Grey |

stimuli.title: Six birthdays from January to June
stimuli.content:
Six persons Aditi, Bhuvan, Charvi, Dhruv, Eshwar and Falguni were born in six different months from January to June of the same (non-leap) year, one person in each month.

- Aditi was born in a month that has 31 days.
- Only one person was born between Aditi and Bhuvan.
- Charvi was born in a month after Bhuvan's.
- Dhruv was born in a month before Falguni's.
- Eshwar was born in a month that has 30 days.
- Falguni was born in the month immediately before Aditi's.
stimuli.solution:
Aditi is in January, March or May. Falguni is immediately before her and Dhruv before Falguni, so Aditi cannot be in January. If Aditi were in May, Bhuvan would be in March, Charvi in June and Falguni in April, leaving no 30-day month (April or June) for Eshwar: rejected. So Aditi = March, Falguni = February, Dhruv = January, Bhuvan = May (January is taken), Charvi = June and Eshwar = April.

| Month | Person |
|---|---|
| January | Dhruv |
| February | Falguni |
| March | Aditi |
| April | Eshwar |
| May | Bhuvan |
| June | Charvi |

stimuli.title: Eight birthdays on the 9th and 24th of four months
stimuli.content:
Eight persons Harini, Imran, Jyoti, Karthik, Madhav, Naina, Omar and Parul have their birthdays in the same year on different dates. Each birthday falls on either the 9th or the 24th of March, June, September or December, and no two persons share a date.

- Harini's birthday is on the 24th of a month that has 30 days.
- Only two persons have birthdays between Harini's and Madhav's.
- Madhav's birthday is in a month that has 31 days.
- Jyoti's birthday comes immediately after Madhav's.
- Imran and Parul have birthdays in the same month, Parul's before Imran's.
- Karthik's birthday is on the 24th and comes before Omar's.
- Naina's birthday is not in June.
stimuli.solution:
Harini is on 24 June or 24 September. Madhav is three dates away in a 31-day month: from 24 June that is 9 March or 9 December; from 24 September it would be 9 June or beyond 24 December, so Harini = 24 June. If Madhav were 9 March (Jyoti 24 March), Imran and Parul would take September or December and Karthik the remaining 24th, leaving no later date for Omar: rejected. So Madhav = 9 December and Jyoti = 24 December. Imran and Parul need a month with both dates free: September (March would leave only 24 September for Karthik and nothing after it for Omar). So Parul = 9 September, Imran = 24 September. Karthik takes 24 March; Naina is not in June, so Naina = 9 March and Omar = 9 June.

| Date | Person |
|---|---|
| 9 March | Naina |
| 24 March | Karthik |
| 9 June | Omar |
| 24 June | Harini |
| 9 September | Parul |
| 24 September | Imran |
| 9 December | Madhav |
| 24 December | Jyoti |

stimuli.title: Seven persons: birth years and professions
stimuli.content:
Seven persons Ashwin, Bharti, Chandan, Damini, Ehsaan, Fiza and Gopal were born in different years among 1968, 1974, 1979, 1985, 1990, 1997 and 2003. Each has a different profession among Architect, Banker, Chef, Doctor, Engineer, Farmer and Lawyer. Ages are calculated as on 2026 (2026 minus the birth year), so the possible ages are 58, 52, 47, 41, 36, 29 and 23.

- Damini's age is a prime number.
- The sum of the ages of Damini and Chandan is 70 years.
- Bharti is older than Fiza, and Fiza was born in an even-numbered year.
- Ehsaan was born in an odd-numbered year after 1990, and Chandan is younger than Ehsaan.
- Ashwin is the Banker, and the Banker is exactly 5 years older than the Architect.
- The Doctor was born in the 1960s.
- The Chef was born in an even-numbered year, and Gopal is not the Chef.
- The Engineer's age is a prime number, and Ehsaan is not the Engineer.
- The Lawyer is exactly 6 years older than the Farmer.
- Damini is not the Architect, and Gopal is younger than Ashwin.
stimuli.solution:
Ehsaan is 1997 or 2003, and Chandan is younger, so Ehsaan = 1997 (29) and Chandan = 2003 (23). Damini's age is 70 − 23 = 47 (prime): 1979. The Banker–Architect gap of 5 years fits 52/47 or 41/36; 47 is Damini, who is not the Architect, so the Banker is 41 (1985: Ashwin) and the Architect is 36 (1990). Gopal is younger than Ashwin, and only 1990 is still free after 1985, so Gopal is the Architect. Bharti and Fiza take 1968 and 1974; Bharti is older, so Bharti = 1968 (the Doctor) and Fiza = 1974. The Lawyer is 6 years older than the Farmer: 29 and 23, so Ehsaan is the Lawyer and Chandan the Farmer. The Engineer's age is prime: Damini (47). Fiza is the Chef (1974 is even).

| Person | Birth year | Age in 2026 | Profession |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bharti | 1968 | 58 | Doctor |
| Fiza | 1974 | 52 | Chef |
| Damini | 1979 | 47 | Engineer |

stimuli.title: Seven officers and seven designations
stimuli.content:
Seven officers Ira, Jeet, Kashvi, Laksh, Mihir, Navya and Pihu of a bank hold seven different posts. In decreasing order of seniority the posts are: General Manager, Deputy General Manager, Assistant General Manager, Chief Manager, Senior Manager, Manager and Assistant Manager.

- Exactly two persons are senior to Pihu.
- Jeet is junior to Pihu but senior to Navya.
- Only one person is designated between Jeet and Kashvi.
- Laksh is junior to both Kashvi and Jeet.
- Ira is immediately junior to Mihir.
- Navya is not the Manager.
stimuli.solution:
Pihu is third (Assistant General Manager). Jeet is fourth, fifth or sixth. Jeet fifth: Kashvi would be third (Pihu's) or seventh (leaving no junior post for Laksh): rejected. Jeet sixth: Navya and Laksh are both junior to him and only the seventh post is left: rejected. So Jeet is fourth (Chief Manager) and Kashvi is second or sixth. Kashvi second: nobody can take the first post (Mihir there would push Ira onto Kashvi's post): rejected. So Kashvi is sixth (Manager), Laksh seventh, Navya fifth (junior to Jeet, not the Manager), and Mihir and Ira take the first and second posts.

|---|---|---|
| 1 | General Manager | Mihir |
| 2 | Deputy General Manager | Ira |
| 3 | Assistant General Manager | Pihu |
| 4 | Chief Manager | Jeet |
| 5 | Senior Manager | Navya |
| 6 | Manager | Kashvi |
| 7 | Assistant Manager | Laksh |

stimuli.title: Machine: smallest number left, first word right
stimuli.content:
A word and number arrangement machine, given an input line of words and numbers, rearranges it step by step. In each step, the smallest number not yet arranged is moved to the extreme left of the line, and the word that comes first in alphabetical order among the words not yet arranged is moved to the extreme right of the line. All other elements keep their order. The process stops when every element has been arranged.

Illustration:
Input: train 46 ruby 13 echo 71 nest 28
Step I: 13 train 46 ruby 71 nest 28 echo
Step II: 28 13 train 46 ruby 71 echo nest
Step III: 46 28 13 train 71 echo nest ruby
Step IV: 71 46 28 13 echo nest ruby train
(Step IV is the last step.)

Step II: 39 17 lamp 52 opal 64 kite 85 brick gate
Step III: 52 39 17 lamp opal 64 85 brick gate kite
Step IV: 64 52 39 17 opal 85 brick gate kite lamp
Step V: 85 64 52 39 17 brick gate kite lamp opal

In the question below, some statements are followed by two conclusions. Take the statements to be true even if they seem to be at variance with commonly known facts, and decide which of the conclusions logically follow.

Statements:
All keys are locks.
Only a few locks are chains.
No chain is a ring.

Conclusions:
I. Some keys are not chains.
II. All rings being locks is a possibility.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: Possibility through the unrestricted part of a set
solution.explanation: Keys may lie entirely in the chain part of locks, so 'Some keys are not chains' is not certain (I fails). Rings are barred only from chains; the non-chain part of locks can hold all rings, so II is possible.
steps: All keys are locks; only a few locks are chains (some are, some are not)
I: keys could all be chains (inside the chain part of locks): not definite
II: rings must avoid chains only; locks that are not chains exist ⇒ all rings being locks is possible
solution.final_answer: Option B: Only conclusion II follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
In the question below, some statements are followed by two conclusions. Take the statements to be true even if they seem to be at variance with commonly known facts, and decide which of the conclusions logically follow.

Statements:
Some coins are tokens.
All tokens are chips.
Only a few chips are cards.

Conclusions:
I. Some coins are chips.
II. All chips being cards is a possibility.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: A possibility that contradicts 'only a few' fails
solution.explanation: Some coins are tokens and all tokens are chips, so some coins are chips (I). 'Only a few chips are cards' means some chips are not cards, so all chips can never be cards (II fails).
steps: Some coins are tokens + All tokens are chips ⇒ Some coins are chips: I follows
Only a few chips are cards ⇒ some chips are NOT cards ⇒ 'All chips are cards' is impossible: II does not follow
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only conclusion I follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
In the question below, some statements are followed by two conclusions. Take the statements to be true even if they seem to be at variance with commonly known facts, and decide which of the conclusions logically follow.

Statements:
Only a few metals are alloys.
All alloys are rods.
No rod is a wire.

Conclusions:
I. Some metals are wires.
II. All wires being alloys is a possibility.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: Possibility blocked by a chain of 'All' and 'No'
solution.explanation: Metals that are not alloys are unrestricted, so a metal–wire overlap is possible but not certain (I fails). Every alloy is a rod and no rod is a wire, so no wire can ever be an alloy (II fails).
steps: I: only the alloy part of metals is barred from wires; the rest may or may not be wires: not definite
All alloys are rods + No rod is a wire ⇒ No alloy is a wire
So 'All wires being alloys' is impossible: II does not follow
solution.final_answer: Option C: Neither conclusion I nor II follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
In the question below, some statements are followed by two conclusions. Take the statements to be true even if they seem to be at variance with commonly known facts, and decide which of the conclusions logically follow.

Statements:
Only a few seeds are plants.
All plants are trees.
No tree is a flower.

Conclusions:
I. Some seeds are flowers.
II. No seed is a flower.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Either conclusion I or II follows

solution.explanation: The seeds that are plants are trees and so are not flowers, but the seeds that are not plants are free: they may or may not be flowers. So neither I nor II is certain, yet one of them must hold. Either I or II follows.
steps: Only a few seeds are plants ⇒ some seeds are plants (⊂ trees, not flowers) and some seeds are not plants
Seeds outside plants can be flowers (I true) or not (II true)
I and II are a 'Some' / 'No' pair on the same terms: Either I or II follows
solution.why_others_wrong: Under the four-option rule 'Either' replaces 'Both', which is impossible for contradictory conclusions.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Either conclusion I or II follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: M > N ≥ O = P < Q ≤ R

Conclusions:
I. M > P
II. R > O

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.explanation: M > N ≥ O = P gives M > P. O = P < Q ≤ R gives R > O. Both follow.
steps: I: M > N ≥ O = P → the path has a strict '>' and no reversed sign: M > P, true
II: O = P < Q ≤ R → R > O, true
solution.shortcut: Any path with one strict sign and no opposite sign gives a strict result.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: A ≤ B < C = D ≥ E > F

Conclusions:
I. C > A
II. E < B

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.explanation: A ≤ B < C gives C > A. Between B and E the signs change direction (B < C = D ≥ E), so no relation can be drawn between E and B.
steps: I: A ≤ B < C → C > A, true
II: B < C = D ≥ E: '<' and '≥' point in opposite directions → no relation, not definite
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only conclusion I follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: G ≥ H = J > K ≤ L < M

Conclusions:
I. G > L
II. M > K

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.explanation: From G down to L the signs flip at K (J > K ≤ L), so G and L cannot be compared. K ≤ L < M gives M > K.
steps: I: G ≥ H = J > K ≤ L: opposite signs around K → no relation
II: K ≤ L < M → M > K, true
solution.final_answer: Option B: Only conclusion II follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: S < T ≤ U = V > W ≥ X

Conclusions:
I. S < W
II. X < T

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.explanation: Both comparisons pass through V, where the direction reverses (U = V > W), so neither S and W nor X and T can be compared.
steps: I: S < T ≤ U = V > W: direction reverses at V → no relation
II: X ≤ W < V = U ≥ T: reverses at U → no relation
solution.final_answer: Option C: Neither conclusion I nor II follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: B ≥ C = D ≤ E < F

Conclusions:
I. E > C
II. E = C

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Either conclusion I or II follows

solution.explanation: C = D ≤ E gives E ≥ C: E is either greater than or equal to C, and neither alone is certain. Since I and II together cover '≥' exactly, either I or II follows.
steps: C = D ≤ E → E ≥ C
I (E > C) alone is not certain; II (E = C) alone is not certain
Together they form E ≥ C, which is certain: Either I or II follows
solution.shortcut: When the derived sign is ≥ (or ≤) and the conclusions are the matching > and =, the answer is Either.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Either' replaces 'Both' here (four-option rule), since E > C and E = C cannot both be true.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Either conclusion I or II follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
In the following question, the symbols #, $, &, % and @ are used with these meanings:
'P # Q' means 'P is greater than Q'; 'P $ Q' means 'P is not smaller than Q'; 'P & Q' means 'P is equal to Q'; 'P % Q' means 'P is smaller than Q'; 'P @ Q' means 'P is not greater than Q'.
Assuming the statements to be true, find which of the conclusions I and II is/are definitely true.

Statements: A # B, B $ C, C & D, D @ E

Conclusions:
I. A # D
II. E $ B

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: Decoding symbols, then reading the chain
solution.explanation: Decoded: A > B ≥ C = D ≤ E. So A > D (I follows). Between E and B the direction reverses at D, so E ≥ B is not certain (II does not follow).
steps: Combined: A > B ≥ C = D ≤ E
I: A # D means A > D: A > B ≥ C = D → true
II: E $ B means E ≥ B: E ≥ D = C ≤ B → no relation
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only conclusion I follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: P > Q ≥ R; S < R ≤ T; U = S

Conclusions:
I. P > U
II. T > S

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: Combining several statements into one chain
solution.explanation: Joining the statements: P > Q ≥ R > S = U and T ≥ R > S. So P > U and T > S: both follow.
steps: Combine: P > Q ≥ R > S = U (S < R written as R > S)
I: P > Q ≥ R > S = U → P > U, true
II: T ≥ R > S → T > S, true
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
In the following question, the symbols ©, ★, δ, % and @ are used with these meanings:
'A © B' means 'A is smaller than B'; 'A ★ B' means 'A is equal to B'; 'A δ B' means 'A is either smaller than or equal to B'; 'A % B' means 'A is greater than B'; 'A @ B' means 'A is either greater than or equal to B'.
Assuming the statements to be true, find which of the conclusions I and II is/are definitely true.

Statements: J © K, K ★ L, L δ M, N % L

Conclusions:
I. M % N
II. N % J

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: Decoding symbols, then reading the chain
solution.explanation: Decoded: J < K = L ≤ M and N > L. M and N are both above L but cannot be compared with each other (I fails). N > L = K > J gives N > J (II follows).
steps: J < K = L ≤ M; N > L
I: M > N? Both M and N are only known to be above L: no relation
II: N > L = K > J → N > J, true
solution.final_answer: Option B: Only conclusion II follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
In the following question, the symbols #, $, &, % and @ are used with these meanings:
'P # Q' means 'P is greater than Q'; 'P $ Q' means 'P is not smaller than Q'; 'P & Q' means 'P is equal to Q'; 'P % Q' means 'P is smaller than Q'; 'P @ Q' means 'P is not greater than Q'.
Assuming the statements to be true, find which of the conclusions I and II is/are definitely true.

Statements: F $ G, G & H, H # I

Conclusions:
I. F # H
II. F & H

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Either conclusion I or II follows

solution.explanation: Decoded: F ≥ G = H > I, so F ≥ H. F > H and F = H are each uncertain, but one of them must be true: either I or II follows.
steps: Decode: F ≥ G, G = H, H > I → F ≥ G = H > I
F ≥ H: F > H (I) or F = H (II)
Neither is certain alone; together they cover F ≥ H: Either
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Either' replaces 'Both' (four-option rule): F > H and F = H cannot both hold.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Either conclusion I or II follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: W ≤ X < Y; Z > Y; V ≥ X; U = V

Conclusions:
I. U > W
II. Z > V

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: Combining several statements into one chain
solution.explanation: U = V ≥ X ≥ W gives only U ≥ W, so U > W is not certain. Z > Y > X and V ≥ X do not compare Z with V.
steps: Chains: W ≤ X < Y < Z, and U = V ≥ X
I: U = V ≥ X ≥ W → U ≥ W only (equality possible): not definite
II: Z and V are both above X, through different branches: no relation
solution.final_answer: Option C: Neither conclusion I nor II follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
In the following question, 'A ¥ B' means 'A is less than B', 'A ∆ B' means 'A is more than B', 'A ◘ B' means 'A is at least B', 'A Ω B' means 'A is at most B', and 'A € B' means 'A and B are equal'.
Assuming the statements to be true, find which of the conclusions I and II is/are definitely true.

Statements: R Ω S, S ¥ T, T € U, V ∆ U

Conclusions:
I. S ∆ V
II. R ¥ U

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: Decoding symbols, then reading the chain
solution.explanation: Decoded: R ≤ S < T = U < V. So S < V, which makes 'S > V' false (I fails), and R < U (II follows).
steps: Decode: R Ω S → R ≤ S, S ¥ T → S < T, T € U → T = U, V ∆ U → V > U
Chain: R ≤ S < T = U < V
I: S ∆ V means S > V, but S < T = U < V: false
II: R ≤ S < T = U → R < U, true
solution.final_answer: Option B: Only conclusion II follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
In the following question, the symbols ◊, ■, ▲, ● and ✱ are used with these meanings:
'A ◊ B' means 'A is neither greater than nor equal to B'; 'A ■ B' means 'A is neither smaller than nor equal to B'; 'A ▲ B' means 'A is not greater than B'; 'A ● B' means 'A is not smaller than B'; 'A ✱ B' means 'A is neither greater than nor smaller than B'.
Assuming the statements to be true, find which of the conclusions I and II is/are definitely true.

Statements: M ● N, N ✱ O, O ■ P, Q ▲ P, Q ◊ R

Conclusions:
I. M ■ Q
II. R ■ P

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: Negative-worded codes ('neither greater nor equal' = smaller)
solution.explanation: Decoded: M ≥ N = O > P ≥ Q < R. M > Q follows. R and P are both compared only with Q (R > Q, P ≥ Q), so they cannot be compared.
steps: M ≥ N = O > P, Q ≤ P, Q < R → M ≥ N = O > P ≥ Q < R
I: M > Q: M ≥ N = O > P ≥ Q → true
II: R > P: R > Q ≤ P → no relation
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only conclusion I follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Which of the following sets of symbols, filled in order in the blanks of the expression below, makes both 'P > T' and 'S ≥ R' definitely true?

P __ Q __ R __ S __ T

solution.concept: Building an expression that forces given conclusions
solution.explanation: With ≥, >, =, ≥ the expression is P ≥ Q > R = S ≥ T. The path from P to T contains a strict '>' and no reversed sign, so P > T; and R = S gives S ≥ R. Every other option fails at least one conclusion.
steps: Option '≥, >, =, ≥': P ≥ Q > R = S ≥ T → P > T and S = R (so S ≥ R): both true
Option '≥, ≥, <, >': P ≥ Q ≥ R < S > T → direction reverses at R and S: P > T fails
Option '>, ≥, ≤, >': P > Q ≥ R ≤ S > T → reverses at R: P > T fails
Option '=, >, <, =': P = Q > R < S = T → reverses at R: P > T fails
solution.shortcut: For P > T the four signs must all point the same way with at least one strict sign; only the first option has no reversal.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: D > E ≥ F; G ≤ F; H = G; I ≥ D

Conclusions:
I. I > H
II. E ≥ H

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: Combining four statements into one chain
solution.explanation: Combined: I ≥ D > E ≥ F ≥ G = H. So I > H (the path contains D > E) and E ≥ H.
steps: Combine: I ≥ D > E ≥ F ≥ G = H
I: I ≥ D > E ≥ F ≥ G = H → I > H (one strict sign), true
II: E ≥ F ≥ G = H → E ≥ H, true
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
In the following question, 'A ⊕ B' means 'A is not greater than B', 'A ⊗ B' means 'A is greater than B', 'A ⊘ B' means 'A is equal to B', 'A ⊙ B' means 'A is not smaller than B', and 'A ⊖ B' means 'A is smaller than B'.
Assuming the statements to be true, find which of the conclusions I and II is/are definitely true.

Statements: T ⊕ U, U ⊗ V, V ⊘ W, X ⊙ U, Y ⊖ W

Conclusions:
I. T ⊖ X
II. Y ⊖ T

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.explanation: Decoded: T ≤ U ≤ X, U > V = W > Y. T ≤ U ≤ X gives only T ≤ X, so T < X is not certain. Y and T are both below U but along different branches, so they cannot be compared.
steps: Decode: T ≤ U, U > V, V = W, X ≥ U, Y < W
T ≤ U ≤ X and U > V = W > Y
I: T < X? Only T ≤ X is certain (T = U = X possible): not definite
II: Y < T? T ≤ U and Y < W < U: both below U, no relation
solution.final_answer: Option C: Neither conclusion I nor II follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: B ≥ C; C > D; E ≤ D; F = E; B ≤ G

Conclusions:
I. G > F
II. D ≥ F

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: Combining five statements into one chain
solution.explanation: Combined: G ≥ B ≥ C > D ≥ E = F. The path from G to F contains the strict sign C > D, so G > F. D ≥ E = F gives D ≥ F. Both follow.
steps: Rewrite each statement in one direction: G ≥ B, B ≥ C, C > D, D ≥ E, E = F
Combined: G ≥ B ≥ C > D ≥ E = F
I: G > F (one strict sign, no reversal): true
II: D ≥ E = F → D ≥ F: true
solution.why_others_wrong: Students who stop at G ≥ B ≥ C often miss that C > D makes the G–F relation strict.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Pointing to a man, Neha said, "His mother is the only daughter of my mother." How is Neha related to the man?

solution.concept: Decoding a pointing statement from the speaker outward
solution.explanation: 'The only daughter of my mother' is Neha herself (a woman speaking about her own mother's only daughter). So the man's mother is Neha.
steps: Speaker: Neha (female)
Only daughter of Neha's mother = Neha
The man's mother = Neha
So Neha is the man's mother
solution.shortcut: When a woman says 'only daughter of my mother', it is herself.
solution.why_others_wrong: Sister or aunt would need the 'only daughter' to be someone other than Neha.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: A is the brother of B. B is the daughter of C. D is the father of C. How is A related to D?

solution.explanation: A and B are siblings, so A is also C's child. D is C's father, so A, a male one generation below C, is D's grandson.
steps: A brother of B, B child of C ⇒ A is C's son
D is C's father ⇒ D is two generations above A
A is male ⇒ grandson

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Ravi's father is Suresh. Suresh's sister is Kamla, and Kamla's husband is Mohan. How is Mohan related to Ravi?

solution.explanation: Kamla is Ravi's father's sister, i.e. his aunt; her husband Mohan is Ravi's uncle.
steps: Suresh → father of Ravi
Kamla → sister of Suresh → Ravi's aunt
Mohan → husband of Kamla → Ravi's uncle

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

solution.concept: Decoding a coded relation chain left to right
solution.explanation: M is the son of N, and N is the wife of O, so M is O's son. O is the father of P, and P is the sister of Q, so Q is also O's child. M and Q are children of the same parents, and M is male: M is Q's brother.
steps: M ÷ N: M is the son of N
N × O: N is the wife of O ⇒ M is the son of O and N
O + P: O is the father of P; P − Q: P is the sister of Q ⇒ Q is also O's child
M (male) and Q share parents ⇒ M is Q's brother

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Introducing a woman, Arun said, "She is the wife of the only grandson of my father's father." How is the woman related to Arun?

solution.explanation: Arun is a grandson of his own father's father. If that man has only one grandson, it must be Arun himself. So the woman is the wife of Arun.
steps: My father's father = Arun's paternal grandfather
His only grandson = Arun (Arun is male and is his grandson)
Wife of that grandson = Arun's wife
solution.why_others_wrong: Sister-in-law would need the grandson to be Arun's brother, but the grandson is unique and Arun is himself a grandson.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
There are six members P, Q, R, S, T and U in a family of three generations, with two married couples.
- Q is the father-in-law of T.
- S is the grandmother of R.
- U is the sister of P.
- R is the son of T.
- Q is married to S, and P is the only son of Q.

How is U related to R?

solution.explanation: Q and S are the grandparents. P is their only son and is married to T (T is Q's daughter-in-law). R is the son of P and T. U is P's sister, so U is R's father's sister: his aunt.
steps: Q is T's father-in-law and P is Q's only son ⇒ T is P's wife
R is T's son ⇒ R is P's son; S (Q's wife) is R's grandmother
U is P's sister ⇒ U is R's paternal aunt

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

solution.explanation: K is L's brother and L is M's daughter, so K is M's son. M is N's husband, so N is K's mother.
steps: K # L: K is the brother of L
L & M: L is the daughter of M ⇒ K is M's son
M $ N: M is the husband of N ⇒ N is the mother of K and L
N @ O: N is O's mother (not needed for the question)

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
A family of three generations has eight members: Harsh, Gita, Kunal, Lata, Meena, Naresh, Om and Pari. There are three married couples, and each couple of the second generation has exactly one child.
- Om is the grandson of Gita.
- Meena is the daughter-in-law of Harsh.
- Pari is the niece of Kunal.
- Naresh is the son-in-law of Gita.
- Lata is the sister of Kunal.
- Harsh is the husband of Gita, and they have only two children.
- Om is the son of Meena.

How is Om related to Lata?

solution.explanation: Harsh and Gita have two children, Kunal and Lata. Meena is Harsh's daughter-in-law, so she is Kunal's wife; Om is their son. Naresh is Gita's son-in-law, so he is Lata's husband, and Pari (Kunal's niece) is their daughter. Om is the son of Lata's brother: her nephew.
steps: Generation 1: Harsh + Gita; children: Kunal, Lata
Meena = Kunal's wife (daughter-in-law of Harsh); their son = Om
Naresh = Lata's husband (son-in-law of Gita); their daughter = Pari (Kunal's niece)
Om is the son of Lata's brother ⇒ nephew
solution.why_others_wrong: Cousin is Om's relation to Pari, not to Lata; grandson is his relation to Harsh and Gita.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

solution.explanation: G is the father of H and I (H is I's sister). J is G's wife and I is J's son, so J is I's mother. K is J's mother, so K is I's maternal grandmother and I, a male, is K's grandson.
steps: G ★ H ● I: G is the father of H; H is the sister of I ⇒ G is I's father
J ▲ G and I ◆ J: J is G's wife and I's mother; I is male
K ■ J: K is J's mother
So K is I's grandmother and I is K's grandson

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
In a family of seven members of three generations — Bhanu, Chhaya, Dev, Esha, Farah, Gagan and Hina — there are two married couples.
- Hina is the granddaughter of Bhanu.
- Farah is the mother of Gagan.
- Esha is the only daughter of Chhaya.
- Dev is the son of Bhanu, and Bhanu has only one son.
- Gagan is the brother of Hina.
- Chhaya is the wife of Bhanu.
- Esha is unmarried.

How is Esha related to the mother of Gagan?

solution.explanation: Bhanu and Chhaya have two children, Dev and Esha. The grandchildren Gagan and Hina must be Dev's children (Esha is unmarried), so Farah is Dev's wife. Esha is the sister of Farah's husband: her sister-in-law.
steps: Generation 1: Bhanu + Chhaya; children Dev (only son) and Esha (only daughter)
Gagan and Hina are grandchildren of Bhanu; Esha is unmarried ⇒ they are Dev's children ⇒ Farah is Dev's wife
Esha = sister of Farah's husband ⇒ sister-in-law
solution.why_others_wrong: Aunt is Esha's relation to Gagan and Hina, not to their mother.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Ravi walks 10 m towards the north. He then turns right and walks 6 m, and then turns right again and walks 4 m. How far is he now from his starting point, and in which direction?

solution.explanation: Net movement: 6 m east and 10 − 4 = 6 m north. Distance = √(6² + 6²) = 6√2 m (about 8.49 m), towards the north-east of the start.
steps: Start (0, 0); 10 m north → (0, 10)
Turn right (now facing east), 6 m → (6, 10)
Turn right (now facing south), 4 m → (6, 6)
Distance = √(36 + 36) = 6√2 m; x > 0 and y > 0 → North-East

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Point A is 5 m west of point B. Point C is 8 m north of point B. Point D is 5 m east of point C. In which direction is point A with respect to point D?

solution.explanation: Taking B as (0, 0): A = (−5, 0), C = (0, 8), D = (5, 8). From D to A the move is 10 m west and 8 m south, so A is to the south-west of D.
steps: A − D = (−10, −8): west and south ⇒ South-West

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: One morning after sunrise, Neeraj was standing facing a pole. The shadow of the pole fell exactly to his right. Which direction was Neeraj facing?

solution.explanation: In the morning the sun is in the east, so shadows fall towards the west. The shadow is on Neeraj's right, so his right hand points west, which means he is facing south.
steps: Morning sun → east; shadow → west
Shadow on his right ⇒ his right = west
Facing south, the right hand points west ⇒ he faces South
solution.shortcut: Morning: shadow west. Whatever side the shadow is on tells you where that hand points.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Starting from her house, Kiran drives 7 km towards the east. She then turns left and drives 9 km, turns right and drives 5 km, and finally turns right and drives 4 km. What is the shortest distance between her house and her present position?

solution.explanation: East: 7 + 5 = 12 km. North: 9 − 4 = 5 km. Shortest distance = √(12² + 5²) = 13 km.
steps: 7 km east → (7, 0)

solution.concept: Shadows in the evening, two observers
solution.explanation: In the evening the sun is in the west, so shadows fall to the east. Asha's shadow is on Bela's left, so Bela's left points east and Bela faces south. Asha faces Bela, so Asha faces north.
steps: Evening sun → west; shadows → east

questions.question_text: A man is facing north-west. He turns 90° clockwise, then 180° anticlockwise, and then 135° clockwise. Which direction is he facing now?

solution.explanation: Measure directions clockwise from north: north-west = 315°. 315 + 90 − 180 + 135 = 360°, i.e. north.
steps: North-west = 315°
+90° → 45° (north-east)
−180° → 225° (south-west)
solution.shortcut: Net turn = 90 − 180 + 135 = 45° clockwise; north-west turned 45° clockwise is north.

questions.question_text: Rohit and Sohan start from the same point X. Rohit walks 10 m east, turns left and walks 6 m, then turns left again and walks 4 m. solution.explanation: Rohit ends at (6, 6) and Sohan at (−6, 15). Sohan − Rohit = (−12, 9), so the distance is √(144 + 81) = 15 m and Sohan is to the north-west of Rohit.

Sohan: west 6 → (−6, 0) → right (north) 15 → (−6, 15)

questions.question_text: In a certain code, BRANCH is written as IDOBSC. How is LOAN written in that code?

Sentences 2 & 4: grows = pe

steps: CHA → AHC, P stays, TER → RET (matches)

DEPOSIT → PEDOTIS

| Code | 7 | % | 2 | @ | 5 | 9 | # | 4 | © | 8 |

Conditions (apply only the first one that fits):
(i) If the first letter is a vowel and the last letter is a consonant, the codes of the first and last letters are interchanged.
(ii) If the first letter is a consonant and the last letter is a vowel, both are coded as the code of the vowel.
(iii) If both the first and the last letters are consonants, both are coded as ★.

What is the code for the letter group PADKER?

solution.explanation: PADKER begins with P and ends with R, both consonants, so condition (iii) applies: both end letters become ★, and the middle letters keep their table codes (A 7, D %, K 5, E 2).
steps: First letter P (consonant), last letter R (consonant): condition (iii)
Middle: A → 7, D → %, K → 5, E → 2

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
In a certain code language:
'risk free bond yield' is written as 'ga lo mi tu',
'bond yield rises' is written as 'mi tu ve',
'free credit offer' is written as 'lo pa ke', and
'credit risk rises' is written as 'pa ga ve'.
What is the code for 'risk offer'?

solution.concept: Multi-step elimination (codes may appear in any order)
solution.explanation: bond and yield take mi and tu (sentences 1 and 2), so rises = ve. free = lo (sentences 1 and 3), credit = pa (sentences 3 and 4), so risk = ga (the remaining code of sentence 4) and offer = ke (the remaining code of sentence 3). 'risk offer' = 'ga ke'.
steps: Sentences 1 & 2: {bond, yield} = {mi, tu} ⇒ rises = ve
Sentences 1 & 3: free = lo
Sentences 3 & 4: credit = pa
Sentence 4: credit pa, rises ve ⇒ risk = ga
Sentence 3: free lo, credit pa ⇒ offer = ke
risk offer = ga ke
solution.why_others_wrong: 'mi ke' fails because mi belongs to bond or yield, which cannot be told apart.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, each vowel of a word is replaced by the letter two places after it in the English alphabet, each consonant by the letter immediately before it, and the resulting letters are then written in reverse order. For example, BANK is written as JMCA. How is CLIENT written in that code?

CLIENT: consonants −1 (C→B, L→K, N→M, T→S); vowels +2 (I→K, E→G)
BKKGMS → reverse → SMGKKB
solution.why_others_wrong: BKKGMS skips the reversal; the other two mis-shift one letter.

Six persons Nikhil, Oorja, Prem, Ritika, Shaan and Trisha have different weights, each a whole number of kilograms.

- Ritika is heavier than Prem but lighter than Shaan.
- Nikhil is lighter than Oorja, and Oorja is heavier than Ritika.
- Trisha is the lightest, and Oorja is not the heaviest.
- The heaviest person weighs 82 kg and the lightest 48 kg.
- Ritika weighs 67 kg and Nikhil 55 kg.

What is the minimum possible combined weight of Oorja and Prem?

solution.concept: Ordering, then the tightest integer bounds
solution.explanation: The order is Shaan > Oorja > Ritika > Prem > Nikhil > Trisha. Oorja must be above Ritika (67), so at least 68 kg; Prem must be above Nikhil (55), so at least 56 kg. Minimum total = 68 + 56 = 124 kg.

Ritika > Prem and Oorja > Ritika, Nikhil < Oorja: the only person who can be below Prem besides Trisha is Nikhil
Ritika, Oorja and Shaan take the top three places with Ritika lowest; Oorja is not the heaviest, so Shaan is
Order: Shaan 82 > Oorja > Ritika 67 > Prem > Nikhil 55 > Trisha 48
Oorja ≥ 68, Prem ≥ 56 ⇒ minimum 124 kg
solution.why_others_wrong: 122 kg uses 67 and 55 themselves, but weights are all different.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by two statements, I and II. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.

Question: Among P, Q, R, S and T, each of a different height, who is the tallest?

I. S is taller than P, and P is taller than both Q and R.
II. T is shorter than Q.

options.text: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not sufficient
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not sufficient
Statements I and II together are not sufficient
Both statements I and II together are necessary

solution.concept: Data sufficiency: test each statement alone, then together
solution.explanation: I alone leaves T unplaced, so S or T could be the tallest. II alone says nothing about P, R or S. Together, T is below Q, which is below P and S, so S is the tallest.
steps: I: S > P > Q, P > R; T unknown → tallest is S or T: not sufficient
II: T < Q only: not sufficient
I + II: S > P > Q > T and P > R → S is tallest: sufficient
Both statements together are necessary
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both statements I and II together are necessary

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

II. Village N is to the north-west of village M.

options.text: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not sufficient
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not sufficient
Either statement I alone or statement II alone is sufficient
Both statements I and II together are necessary

solution.concept: Data sufficiency: test each statement alone, then together
solution.explanation: From I, M is 4 km east and 4 km south of N, i.e. south-east. From II, if N is north-west of M then M is south-east of N. Each statement alone answers the question.
steps: I: N (0, 0) → P (0, −4) → M (4, −4): M is South-East of N: sufficient
II: N is North-West of M ⇒ M is South-East of N: sufficient
Either statement alone is sufficient
solution.final_answer: Option C: Either statement I alone or statement II alone is sufficient

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by two statements, I and II. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.

II. B sits immediately to the left of E, and F sits at the extreme left end.

options.text: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not sufficient
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not sufficient
Either statement I alone or statement II alone is sufficient
Both statements I and II together are necessary

solution.concept: Data sufficiency: test each statement alone, then together
solution.explanation: From I, C is at seat 3 and E, three seats away, must be at seat 6 (seat 0 does not exist): E is at the right end. II fixes only F and the B–E pair, which can sit in several places.
steps: I: C = 3; E = 3 ± 3 → E = 6 ⇒ E sits at the extreme right: sufficient
II: F = 1; B–E adjacent anywhere from seats 2–3 to 5–6: not sufficient
I alone is sufficient
solution.final_answer: Option A: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not sufficient

Statements I and II together are not sufficient
Both statements I and II together are necessary

steps: I: gold and rise ↔ {tu, pa} (rate = ka): not sufficient
II: gold and rise ↔ {pa, tu} (coin = ro): not sufficient

Even together the statements are not sufficient

Statements I and II together are not sufficient

solution.explanation: I leaves Thursday and Friday open. From II, the brother visited on Wednesday, so Mohan visited on Thursday.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by three statements, I, II and III. Decide which of the statements are sufficient to answer the question.

Question: Among P, Q, R, S and T, each of a different age, who is the oldest?

I. P is older than both Q and R.
II. S is older than P.
III. T is younger than Q.

options.text: Only statements I and II together are sufficient
Only statements I and III together are sufficient
All three statements I, II and III together are necessary
Even all three statements together are not sufficient

solution.concept: Three-statement data sufficiency: test every pair before using all three
solution.explanation: No single statement or pair is enough: I + II leaves T unplaced; I + III leaves S unplaced; II + III leaves Q and R free. With all three, S > P > Q > T and P > R, so S is the oldest.
steps: Any single statement: clearly insufficient
I + II: S > P > Q, R; T could be older than S: not sufficient
I + III: P > Q > T, P > R; S unknown: not sufficient
II + III: S > P, Q > T; Q or R could be oldest: not sufficient
I + II + III: S > P > Q > T and P > R ⇒ S oldest: all three are necessary
solution.final_answer: Option C: All three statements I, II and III together are necessary

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by three statements, I, II and III. Decide which of the statements are sufficient to answer the question.

Question: Six friends A, B, C, D, E and F sit around a circular table, equally spaced and facing the centre. Who sits opposite A?

I. C sits second to the left of A.
II. D is an immediate neighbour of both C and F.
III. B sits immediately to the right of A.

options.text: Only statements I and II together are sufficient
Only statements II and III together are sufficient
All three statements I, II and III together are necessary
Any two of the three statements together are sufficient

solution.concept: Three-statement data sufficiency with a circular arrangement
solution.explanation: With I, C is two seats to A's left, which is next to the seat opposite A. II then needs D between C and F: D cannot sit on the side towards A (F would have to take A's seat), so D sits opposite A. So I and II together answer the question. III only places B next to A and does not complete any other combination.
steps: Number the seats 0–5 to A's right (A = 0, opposite A = 3)
I: C = 4. II alone: no fixed seat. III: B = 1
I + II: D beside C → seat 3 or 5; D = 5 would need F at seat 0 (A's seat), so D = 3: sufficient
I + III: C = 4, B = 1; seats 2, 3, 5 open for D, E, F: not sufficient
II + III: B = 1 and a C–D–F block elsewhere: not sufficient
Only I and II together are sufficient
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only statements I and II together are sufficient

Read the statement and the two assumptions. An assumption is something supposed or taken for granted by the person making the statement. Decide which of the assumptions is/are implicit in the statement.

solution.explanation: An incentive is offered only if the bank believes it will motivate at least some customers, so I is implicit. II contradicts the very purpose of the offer: if everyone had already registered, no incentive would be needed.
steps: I: the offer makes sense only if a free cheque book attracts some customers: implicit
II: if all had registered, the offer would be pointless: not implicit

options.text: Neither I nor II is implicit
Both I and II are implicit

steps: I: the notice links tokens with avoiding a long queue: implicit
II: a notice is put up only if people are expected to read and act on it: implicit

II: the company need not assume 100% of staff will relocate: not implicit

options.text: Neither I nor II is implicit
Both I and II are implicit

solution.explanation: The plan is meant to cut cash-handling cost, so the bank assumes the machines can do that (I). It picks the busiest branches because that is where enough cash is handled for the saving to matter (II).
steps: I: the stated goal is cost reduction through the machines: implicit

options.text: Neither I nor II is implicit
Both I and II are implicit

steps: I: the purpose of mandatory prominent disclosure is better comparison: implicit

options.text: Neither I nor II is implicit
Both I and II are implicit
